pharm: Calcium salt; electrolyte replenisher and antacid
quick: Oral 1000-1200 mg elemental Ca/day; IV per hypocalcemia
Carbonate with food; citrate any time
Caution; risk of hypercalcemia and stones
Serum calcium, renal function; ECG for IV
summary: Calcium salts are used orally for dietary supplementation, hypocalcemia and as antacids, and intravenously (gluconate or chloride) for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia-induced cardiotoxicity, calcium-channel-blocker/magnesium toxicity. IV calcium chloride contains ~3x the elemental calcium of gluconate per volume and is more irritating. Key risks are hypercalcemia, arrhythmias (especially with digoxin), and tissue necrosis from extravasation.
indications: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (IV calcium gluconate or chloride)
Dietary calcium supplementation / prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency (oral)
Adjunct in osteoporosis and osteopenia (with vitamin D)
Calcium-channel-blocker overdose and magnesium sulfate toxicity
Hyperphosphatemia phosphate binder in chronic kidney disease (calcium carbonate/acetate)

dosage.d: 1000-2000 mg (1-2 g) calcium gluconate IV; individualized
dosage.t: Slow IV bolus over ~5-10 min then infusion
dosage.n: Measure serum calcium every 4-6 h (intermittent) or 1-4 h (continuous)
Chloride salt ~3x elemental calcium of gluconate; very irritating to veins

dosage.d: Calcium gluconate 1-2 g (or calcium chloride 0.5-1 g) IV
dosage.t: Over 2-5 min, repeat if ECG changes persist
dosage.n: Does not lower potassium; bridge to potassium-lowering therapy

dosage.d: 1000-1200 mg elemental calcium/day in divided doses
dosage.t: Carbonate with meals; citrate any time
dosage.n: Limit single doses to <=500-600 mg elemental for best absorption
Max per labeling; avoid chronic high-dose use
Contraindicated in neonates <=28 days receiving ceftriaxone

admin: IV calcium gluconate may be given as bolus or continuous infusion via a secure IV line; infuse slowly
Calcium chloride is highly irritant - prefer a central or large secure vein; avoid extravasation
Use careful ECG monitoring during IV administration to detect arrhythmias
Do NOT mix calcium with phosphate- or bicarbonate-containing fluids (precipitation)
Do NOT give simultaneously with IV ceftriaxone via Y-site in any age group
Oral: take calcium carbonate with food to improve absorption; separate from interacting drugs
moa: Calcium is essential for nerve conduction, muscle contraction, cardiac function, bone mineralization, and coagulation. IV calcium raises serum ionized calcium, correcting hypocalcemic symptoms and stabilizing the cardiac membrane resting potential in hyperkalemia. Oral calcium carbonate also neutralizes gastric acid and binds dietary phosphate.

absolute: Neonates <=28 days of age receiving ceftriaxone (IV calcium)
Known calcium-containing renal stones (relative-to-absolute depending on salt)
relative: Severe renal impairment / risk of hypercalcemia and nephrolithiasis

preg: Calcium is required for maternal and fetal health and is considered compatible in pregnancy at recommended intakes. IV calcium is used for acute hypocalcemia in pregnancy when indicated.
lact: Calcium is a normal milk constituent; supplementation at recommended intakes is compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment due to risk of hypercalcemia, metastatic calcification and stones. Calcium-based phosphate binders are used in CKD but require monitoring of calcium-phosphate balance.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment.

major: Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - hypercalcemia increases digoxin toxicity; synergistic arrhythmias - avoid IV calcium or give slowly with ECG monitoring
IV ceftriaxone - life-threatening calcium-ceftriaxone precipitates; do not coadminister in neonates and avoid Y-site coadministration in all ages
moderate: Calcium channel blockers - calcium may reduce their effect
Thiazide diuretics, vitamin D, vitamin A, estrogen, calcipotriene, teriparatide - additive hypercalcemia risk
Tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, iron - oral calcium reduces their absorption (separate dosing)
minor: Antacid effect may raise gastric pH and alter absorption of pH-dependent drugs
interactions.food: Oral calcium carbonate is best absorbed with food; high-oxalate/phytate foods and excess fiber can reduce absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic heavy alcohol use impairs calcium absorption and bone health.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause hypercalcemia; monitor serum/ionized calcium. May affect calcium-dependent lab assays.

serious: Hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac arrhythmias with rapid IV
Tissue necrosis, calcinosis cutis and ulceration from extravasation
emergency: Cardiac arrest with rapid IV push

monitoring: Serum (total and ionized) calcium - frequently during IV therapy (every 1-6 h)
ECG during IV administration, especially in cardiac/digoxin patients
IV site for extravasation and tissue injury
Signs/symptoms of hypercalcemia with chronic oral use
counsel: Take oral calcium carbonate with food; space large doses (no more than ~500-600 mg elemental at once)
Separate calcium from thyroid medicine, antibiotics (tetracyclines/quinolones), iron and bisphosphonates by 2+ hours
Report constipation, nausea, confusion, or excessive thirst/urination (possible hypercalcemia)
Maintain adequate fluid intake to reduce kidney-stone risk
Tell your provider if you take digoxin or have kidney disease
pk: IV: immediate rise in serum calcium; oral: gradual
IV: at end of infusion; oral carbonate within a few hours
Regulated by homeostasis (PTH, vitamin D); not a fixed value
IV effect transient (~30 min to hours); replace as needed
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); do not freeze IV solution
pearls: Calcium chloride contains ~3x the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate per equal volume of 10% solution (CaCl2 ~27% vs gluconate ~9% elemental)
In hyperkalemia, IV calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does NOT lower serum potassium - follow with insulin/glucose, etc.
Never mix calcium with bicarbonate or phosphate (precipitation); never coadminister IV with ceftriaxone
Calcium gluconate is preferred peripherally; calcium chloride is more irritating and best given centrally
Hypercalcemia potentiates digoxin toxicity - avoid or use cautiously with ECG monitoring
Elemental content: carbonate ~40%, citrate ~21%, gluconate ~9% by weight
missed: For oral supplementation, take the missed dose when remembered; if it is near the next dose, skip it and do not double up. IV calcium is given for acute indications and is not self-dosed.
overdose: Overdose causes hypercalcemia (symptoms typically at serum calcium >=12 mg/dL): weakness, fatigue, confusion, then hallucinations, seizures and coma; impaired urine concentration and arrhythmias. Stop calcium administration, restore intravascular volume with IV saline, promote urinary calcium excretion, and give additional therapy (e.g., calcitonin, bisphosphonates) for severe hypercalcemia.
